item.title: The 2027 budget: the main measures and what it means for you
item.description:
The 2027 budget: the main measures and what it means for you

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The minority Dutch government published its 2027 budget on Tuesday, outlining the latest economic forecasts and its plans for the coming year. Here are the highlights:

Government and local government finances

  • Inflation will average 2.7% in 2027.
  • Wages will rise by an average of 3.8%.
  • Economic growth will remain in line with earlier projections at 1.2%, without major upsets.
  • The budget deficit will rise to 2.7%, well below the EU maximum of 3%.
  • The government plans to cut €400 million from spending on its own operations, with the aim of a structural reduction of €1 billion from 2030.
  • The local authorities fund will rise marginally to just under €50 billion, or €2,741 per resident.

Taxes

  • Spending power will fall marginally for all but pensioners and low-income households.
  • Plans to reform the Box 3 asset tax system are due in spring 2027.
  • Income tax in the first tax band (up to €39.20) will hit 36.23%, up from 35.75% now.
  • The income tax rate in the second tax band (up to €78,400) will rise from 37.56% to 38.16%
  • The arbeidskorting – a tax break for people in work – will rise slightly.
  • Employers will no longer be able to give workers a 20% discount tax free on the company’s own products.
  • The startersaftrek – a discount for the newly self-employed – will be cut to a nominal €10 in 2027 and scrapped altogether in 2028.
  • Untaxed travel expenses will rise to 25 cents per kilometre and has been backdated to the start of 2026.
  • BTW on plants, flowers and trips by balloon will rise from 9% to 21%.
  • Excise duty on alcohol will rise in line with inflation.

Defence and foreign affairs

  • €600 million extra will go to defence in 2027, taking the total to almost €29 billion, including €3.1 billion in military support for Ukraine.
  • €35 million will be spent on Dutch diplomatic missions abroad, partly offsetting cuts imposed by the last government. The consulate in Antwerp will remain open.
  • The development aid budget will rise by €400 million a year for the next three years, on top of the extra money agreed in June to win senate support and the partial reversal of the Schoof cabinet’s €2.4 billion cuts.
  • The Netherlands will not hit the OECD target of 0.7% of GDP on aid spending.

Benefits

  • Cuts to slash the period for claiming unemployment benefit from two to one year have been delayed until 2029.
  • A planned faster increase in the state pension age will not go ahead.
  • A lower maximum for payouts to pregnant women and people on invalidity benefit will not go ahead.
  • As announced earlier, low income households faced with mounting energy bills will be able to request help from a special energy fund

Healthcare

  • The health insurance own risk payment will rise from €385 to €400 in line with inflation.
  • €100 million is being allocated to ensure 60 to 69-year-olds can be vaccinated against shingles. The over 70s must pick up the bill themselves.
  • The government expects health insurance premiums will rise by €12.50 a month – although health insurance companies decide their own rates.

Housing and infrastructure

  • The housing ministry budget will top €7 billion next year.
  • Of this, €940 million will be allocated to boost major residential developments in terms of facilities and green spaces.
  • €630 million will go to specialised housing for the elderly.
  • From 2028, people who earn too much to live in rent-controlled homes will face bigger rent increases. The check will also include a look at individual assets.
  • Housing corporations will get a €425 million tax cut, allowing them to borrow an extra €6 billion to build social housing.
  • Private investors will be able to claim up to €10,000 for every mid-market rental home they build, from a budget of €500 million running from 2029 to 2033.
  • €1.5 billion has been allocated for road and bridge repairs until 2035.
  • €300 million will be invested annually in improving transport links to new residential developments, beginning in 2030.

Education and research

  • Education will get €668 million extra, largely reversing cuts to higher education imposed by the previous government.
  • There will be more investment in trade schools and in scientific research.
  • Funding is being set aside for the development of a national super computer and an Einstein telescope R&D centre.
  • The basic grant for students living away from home will rise by €50 from 2028.
  • €346 million will go to additional training for teachers from 2028.
  • More money will be allocated to help people shift into teaching from other professions.
  • €23 million is being allocated to provide free fruit in schools that request it.
  • The government will introduce a “sport pass” for 12 to 23-year-olds of €100 to €300 to be invested in sports.

Climate

  • Money will be allocated to help farmers who want to invest in making their businesses more sustainable and climate-friendly.
  • €1.3 billion is being allocated to store carbon dioxide in empty gas fields under the North Sea.
  • New measures to combat climate change will be announced in 2027.

Asylum and migration

  • The government says spending on refugees will reach €8 billion this year but go down to €5 billion by 2031 because of EU and other measures.
  • Local authorities which have not set up their own permanent refugee centres will be placed on a blacklist.
  • €22 million will be invested in setting up refugee centres outside the EU in 2027.
  • More money will be put into dealing with refugees who commit crimes and in secure accommodation for them.

Travel and transport

  • A 10 cent reduction in the price of diesel will be phased out from 2028 not 2027.
  • Tax on long-distance flights is being set at €59 instead of €74 to ensure Schiphol is not more expensive than German airports.

Royals

  • Spending on staff etc. will rise from €60.8 million to €62.1 million in 2027.
  • The king, queen and princess Amalia will have combined income of €2.7 million this year, but Amalia will not claim hers while she is studying.
  • The royals’ income rises in line with civil servant pay, which is 0.3% this year.

This article will be updated as more information becomes available.

item.title: Heinen warns “hard choices” are needed to secure future growth
item.description:
Heinen warns “hard choices” are needed to secure future growth

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Finance minister Eelco Heinen has said the Netherlands needs to build a “coalition for growth” to secure the future prosperity and security of the country.

Heinen said no one party had a monopoly on the answers and his own ideas on the role of markets and European co-operation had been forced to change in response to the challenges to the international order in recent years.

But he warned that the Netherlands also needed to cut its spending and reform social security and healthcare if it wanted to become “the best place to invest and grow”.

“International competition is becoming fiercer, our productivity is hardly growing and investment is lagging behind,” he said.

“Economic growth must become a national challenge, because a country that moves forwards is in everyone’s interest.”

Heinen, who represents the right-wing, fiscally conservative VVD party in the centre-right coalition, said the budget package had made space for the demands of opposition parties on both left and right.

Capital gains

Many of the original plans in the coalition agreement have been watered down or postponed as Heinen seeks support for a “common goal” that goes “beyond the next budget.”

The cabinet will bring forward plans to introduce capital gains tax system to replace the Box 3 asset tax, which the Supreme Court has said violates European human rights laws.

Heinen said the extended discount on fuel duty, cutting airport tax and making air travel more sustainable showed he was prepared to accommodate the wishes of opposition parties.

Social security

But his reference to “hard choices” were a clear signal that he is determined to press ahead with significant cuts to the social security and healthcare budgets, which the largest left-wing party Pro and the trade unions insist must be scrapped.

“Without reforms to social security and healthcare the money we spend today will hold back the growth of the future,” Heinen said.

The minister said the “handbrake” needed to be taken off investment, with the government increasing investment in helping startup businesses “get off the ground and stay here”.

Heinen said his ideas on international co-operation had changed in recent years as he saw the trend in the global economy turning from free trade to the agressive use of economic power.

European co-operation

“You know I believe strongly in the power of the market, but if the market comes up short and promising businesses can’t grow as a result, you have to be prepared to adapt your beliefs to reality,” he said.

International rules were no longer a guarantee of global security and the Netherlands needed to work on strengthening the European Union’s internal economic ties. “Yesterday’s world is not coming back,” he said.

“I will still be critical when Europa claims more influence than it needs or builds up more debts. But co-operation sometimes gives us more influence.

That’s why we must deepen European co-operation and make our internal market work better and improve our ties with countries outside Europe.”

item.title: Opposition parties dismiss king’s speech as road to stagnation
item.description:
Opposition parties dismiss king’s speech as road to stagnation

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Opposition parties have accused the Dutch government of failing to make choices and leading the country into a “stagnation” following a king’s speech packed with appeals to the Dutch traditions of compromise and co-operation.

In a long and wide-ranging speech, King Willem-Alexander said “communality” could be an “antidote to polarisation” and said solutions needed to be found on issues such as nitrogen pollution, the housing crisis and social unrest around asylum.

But opposition parties said the cabinet had failed to set out a clear vision or take the initiative in coming forward with ideas to fix the problems.

“Politics is about making choices,” said Joost Eerdmans, leader of the right-wing conservative JA21. “The king can say democracy isn’t 50% plus one, but that’s how it works in practice. They’ve forgotten to turn left or right, or else they can’t.”

Jesse Klaver, leader of the largest left-wing opposition party Pro, said the king’s “fine words” could not disguise the fact “that the cabinet is rudderless.”

“We are in a permanent process of forming the government because the minority government can’t agree on which way to take the country in.”

Lack of direction

In the weeks before the opening day of parliament the three coalition parties D66, CDA and VVD were unable to agree what concessions to make to opposition parties in the budget deal that finance minister Eelco Heinen will deliver on Tuesday.

Instead the minority government will have to keep negotiating with opposition leaders to find the 10 seats it needs in the lower house and the 16 seats in the Senate to pass its laws.

Mirjam Bikker, leader of the ChristenUnie, said the king’s speech showed a lack of direction from the coalition parties.

“If you want to make progress, you have to decide which way to go,” she said. “We’ve seen a few concessions on minor things like cuts to healthcare, but my concern is that without a sense of direction it’ll just be a few trinkets.”

Geert Wilders of the far-right PVV criticised the speech for failing to address people’s concerns about fundamental issues such as the rising cost of living.

”Lots of money is being spent on Europe, development aid, nitrogen and the climate, while we see the country is changing and we can’t pay the bills,” he said. ”The sooner this cabinet falls, the better.”

item.title: Protecting democracy takes centre stage in king’s speech
item.description:
Protecting democracy takes centre stage in king’s speech

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Democracy was the central theme of king Willem-Alexander’s speech to both houses of parliament on Tuesday afternoon, an event in which the monarch traditionally outlines the main themes of government policy for the coming year.

“Democracy requires constant protection and maintenance,” the king said.

“Everyone who does something for another person – as a volunteer, an unpaid carer or in some other capacity – serves the public interest and makes the Netherlands stronger. Fortunately, this Dutch tradition of community spirit endures, as an antidote to polarisation.”

“That is why it’s so important that we don’t reduce the concept of democracy to the will of half the people plus one. Democracy should unite people, not play them off against each other.

An important element in this, the king said, is ensuring the public have confidence that government will solve their problems. “It is a joint contract with parliament and the government to make sure that their questions can more often be answered by ‘yes’.”

“Parliamentary democracy belongs to everyone, is for everyone and should serve everyone.”

Read the official translation of the speech

The king went on to outline various policy initiatives drawn up by the minority government for the coming years. Some problems, such as the housing shortage, nitrogen-based pollution, public safety and climate change have, he said, been “asking for solutions for far too long.”

The king said the cabinet will continue to listen to the concerns of farmers who are worried about their livelihoods, particularly those working close to areas where nature is under threat. But it would be “irresponsible” to delay measures to reduce nitrogen pollution, he said.

He called for a pragmatic approach to solving the housing crisis, including more reliance on prefabricated buildings. Reducing refugee numbers will take time and he described the wave of protests about the location of refugee centres as “worrying”.

“It must be clear that threats and violence are unacceptable,” he said.

Railway sabotage

The king’s speech took place as the police and railway officials sought to end at least 30 acts of sabotage on the railways, plus numerous hay bale fires close to motorways, thought to have been carried out by militant farmers.

He did not refer to the trouble expressly, but he closed his speech by saying that one definition of democracy includes the need to give way occasionally to the meaning of others.

“The spirit of reasonableness and compromise implied in that remark will solve more problems for people than the constant controversies that sometimes seem to be gaining the upper hand,” he said.

item.title: One in four questions in Dutch parliament “written using AI”
item.description:
One in four questions in Dutch parliament “written using AI”

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Around a quarter of questions from MPs in the Dutch parliament were written with the help of AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude, according to research by broadcaster NOS.

NOS analysed 28,000 questions using the AI detection tool Pangram and found that 26% of them showed stylistic features of AI.

Usage peaked at more than 30% just before the summer recess, but dropped to around 17% in July, roughly the same level as a year go.

Some MPs included a sentence or two of AI, while others used to generate whole strings of questions.

Last week prime minister Rob Jetten was criticised after it emerged that around 30% of his social media posts included AI-generated content.

Some of the messages were apparently personal reflections on sensitive subjects such as the mistreatment of Moluccan war veterans in the 1950s, which Jetten recently apologised for on behalf of the government.

Jetten defended the practice, saying that “like three-quarters of Dutch people I sometimes use AI to make things better”.

The use of AI to formulate questions is not necessarily a problem, according to some experts. “If MPs weren’t using it at all I would see that as a bad thing,” AI developer Maarten Sukel told NOS.

But he said it should not be used as a short-cut for in-depth research. “If you’re working on a dossier that you don’t know so much about and you let AI help you come up with questions to ask in parliament, that’s a problem.”

“Faster and smarter”

MP Daniël van den Berg, of the right-wing opposition party JA21, said: “I think it would be a shame for me to spend hours trawling through minutes and documents looking for media items. AI helps me do it faster and smarter.”

But Marleen Stikker, founder of De Digitale Stad, one of the Netherlands’ first online networks, said using AI in parliament undermined Dutch democracy.

“We are outsourcing our democratic system to the American AI companies’ algorithms, which aren’t even neutral, they’re skewed. That’s absurd, surely?”

item.title: Children in Dutch care system exploited on placements abroad
item.description:
Children in Dutch care system exploited on placements abroad

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Children in the Dutch care system may be being exploited while on youth placements abroad, an investigation by current affairs programme Nieuwsuur has found.

Councils and child protection agencies can sometimes send children with behavioural problems to other countries, such as Spain, when there is no suitable place for them in the Netherlands. This is supposed to be a temporary solution but some end up staying for up to three years.

The investigation found that the health and youth care inspectorate (IGJ) has been flagging risks in the system since 2009, but parliament was never informed. The inspectorate now says it is receiving reports of children being forced into unpaid work, locked up and not going to school, and admits that nothing has changed.

Because the IGJ has no jurisdiction in foreign countries it cannot investigate reports itself. Some children are also being sent outside the EU, the investigation found, some to Morocco.

Those placed in Morocco have no background in the country, which the organisation running the site, Multi Plus Zorg, said is an advantage because it makes the children more dependent on staff and lets them focus on their own development. Youth law professor Mariëlle Bruning told the programme it “smells of abuse”.

The IGJ said “peer pressure” was being used in some places to keep children under control, and that some were subjected to “outdated” methods focused on punishment.

It also said it has reports of children being physically restrained and barred from leaving the grounds, neither of which is permitted in this type of care, and of some having to do heavy work instead of going to school.

The inspectorate last counted how many Dutch children were in care abroad in 2007, when there were 330.

Youth care minister Mirjam Sterk said she found the situation “worrying”. Parliament passed a motion earlier this year to limit placements abroad as far as possible.

item.title: Croatian couple on run from Slovenia arrested near Dutch border
item.description:
Croatian couple on run from Slovenia arrested near Dutch border

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A Croatian couple who went into hiding in the Netherlands after being sought in connection with a murder in Slovenia have been arrested across the border in Germany.

The 31-year-old man and 29-year-old woman were stopped in a car park Isterberg, near the border town of Nordhorn, on Friday evening. They were driving a car with Slovakian numberplates that turned out to have been stolen from another vehicle.

The Telegraaf reported that the couple had been living in the Netherlands prior to their arrest. Police believe they had just crossed the border from the Netherlands because strict checks are in place on the German side.

A check on the couple revealed that prosecutors in Slovenia had issued a European arrest warrant for the couple, who are suspected of beating, strangling and murdering their victim.

They spent Friday night in a police cell in Nordhorn before appearing in court the next morning, where a district judge ordered them to be transferred to prison in Oldenburg prison, where they are expected to face an extradition hearing.

item.title: Three Dutch die in small airplane crash in Germany
item.description:
Three Dutch die in small airplane crash in Germany

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A small aircraft carrying three Dutch people crashed in Erkelenz, not far from the German border near Roermand. Local police confirmed all three were dead at the scene on Monday morning.

The victims were a 57-year-old man from the Súdwest-Fryslân area of Friesland, and a 58-year-old man and a 23-year-old woman, both from Amsterdam, the foreign affairs ministry told broadcaster NOS. Their names have not been released but next of kin have been notified, the ministry said.

The plane, a four-seat Cessna 172, belonged to Vliegschool Hilversum, a flight school based at the airfield outside Hilversum. Flight tracking data show it took off at 10.25am and disappeared from radar at 11.18am near Erkelenz.

The school released a statement: “With great concern we announce that an accident has occurred in Germany involving one of our aircraft, a Cessna 172. The circumstances of the incident are still unclear.”

The school has halted all its flights while the investigation into the crash is ongoing. The purpose of the flight, and what caused it to crash, has not been made clear.

Dutch aviation safety investigators are joining German authorities to establish what happened, broadcaster NOS reported.

German media reports indicate that the plane may have been on route to Freiburg, and that the pilot had contacted air traffic control due to bad weather before the plane began losing altitude and crashed.

item.title: Far-right party school research was misleading, experts say
item.description:
Far-right party school research was misleading, experts say

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The research which led the government to put €507,000 into a primary school backed by far-right party Forum voor Democratie was flawed and did not include key information, experts have told the Volkskrant.

The Renaissance school opened its doors in Almere this school year with just four pupils, well below the number required for official funding. But officials agreed to back the school because research apparently showed there would be a demand for new schools in the area over the coming years.

However, Peter Kanne from market research bureau Ipsos I&O told the Volkskrant that the questionnaire did not tell prospective parents the school was allied to the party and instead asked general questions about their thoughts on education.

Some 35,000 invitations to take part in the research were sent to the homes in the Almere Oosterwold area – which is several kilometres from the school’s location.

In total 258 parents responded and 18 parents said they would like their child to attend the school, the Volkskrant said, after using freedom of information legislation.

That percentage is extremely low, making it impossible to determine if the research was representative, professor Tom Louwerse told the paper. “This research says little or nothing about the potential of the school,” he said.

Experts also criticised the questioning, in which parents were asked to choose options such as “a focus on reading and arithmetic” and “lessons five days a week” – which all Dutch schools offer. Nor did the survey mention that girls and boys will be taught differently.

The education ministry said in response to MPs’ questions earlier that all the rules for the research had been followed.

D66 parliamentarian Ilana Rooderkerk told the paper the school was launched “under false pretences” and has submitted a string of questions to the minister. “We need to ditch this sort of misleading research,” she said. “Children should never become the subject of a political project.”

An earlier attempt to open a Renaissance school in Almere, which was fully funded by parents and private sources, failed and closed in 2024.

item.title: Unrest in Rotterdam after man dies in mistaken arrest
item.description:
Unrest in Rotterdam after man dies in mistaken arrest

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The death of a Rotterdam man who was arrested by police on Saturday for purportedly riding a stolen fatbike has sparked unrest in the city after it turned out he was not who they were looking for. Police confirmed that his fatbike was the wrong one, and prosecutors said he resisted arrest and then died shortly afterwards despite their attempts to resuscitate him.

The 51-year old, Alfredo Goeloe, was out to collect diabetes medication, according to his family, when police approached as they were searching for a stolen fatbike.

He failed to produce identification, public prosecutors said, and ran from them. Once they caught him he tried to escape their restraints and then fell immediately unwell.

Some of the events were caught on camera, including him screaming in pain and shouting that he had diabetes as additional police rushed to assist the arrest.

A 45-second video of the event, which cut off before he fell ill, was taken by a passer by. The footage is being investigated and Goeloe’s relatives are being assisted by an organisation called Controle Alt Delete, which works against ethnic profiling.

His family’s lawyer also told the talk show Pauw en de Wit on Monday night that they will file a criminal complaint. Goeloe’s partner is expecting a child.

A silent march in Rotterdam was held last night in tribute to Goeloe, which proceeded peacefully but ended with some unrest outside the Zuidplein police station, where riot police formed a line in front of the marchers and fireworks were thrown. One person was arrested.
